unit.title: Materials
unit.blurb: Solids, liquids and gases, melting and freezing, and fizzy reactions in the kitchen.

O1.t: Name common materials, and sort materials into solids, liquids and gases; know that everything is made of tiny particles.

O2.t: Know that solids keep their shape, and liquids flow and take the shape of their container.

O3.t: Know that heating can melt solids and cooling can make liquids solidify (freeze).

O4.t: Know that a chemical reaction makes a new material, and spot signs of a reaction (bubbles, colour, heat, smell).

captions: Hello, material masters!
Everything around you is made of materials.
This is lesson 3.1: materials and particles.
Look around your room.
A chair can be made of wood.
A cup can be made of plastic. A window is made of glass.
And a spoon is made of metal. Wood, plastic, glass and metal are materials.
Materials can be solid, liquid or gas.
Ice is a solid. It keeps its shape.
Water is a liquid. It flows.
The air is a gas. It spreads out everywhere.
Pause and think.
Is ice a solid, a liquid, or a gas?
Everything is made of tiny particles, too small to see.
In a solid, the particles are packed tightly together.
In a liquid, the particles can slide past each other.
In a gas, the particles are far apart, and zoom around!
Did you know?
When you blow up a balloon, you fill it with gas.
The gas particles push on the inside, and keep the balloon round!
Joke time!
What can you catch, but not throw?
A cold! Achoo!
Your turn.
Which of these is a liquid?
Let's go on a material hunt!
Find ten things in your home.
What is each one made of? Is it a solid, a liquid or a gas?
Sort them into groups.
Let's remember.
Everything is made of materials.
Materials can be solid, liquid or gas.
Everything is made of tiny particles.
In a gas, the particles are far apart. Marvellous work!

captions: Hello, material masters!
Solids and liquids behave in different ways.
This is lesson 3.2: how solids and liquids behave.
Put a brick on the table. It keeps its shape.
Now pour some juice. It flows!
The juice takes the shape of the glass. That glass is its container.
Solids keep their shape. Liquids flow and take the shape of their container.
Pause and think.
What happens when you pour a liquid into a glass?
Some things are tricky!
You can pour rice, like a liquid.
But look closely. Each tiny grain keeps its shape. Rice is a solid!
Honey is a liquid. It flows, but very slowly.
Let's sort some more.
An apple is a solid. Milk is a liquid.
Salt is a solid, made of tiny grains.
And oil is a liquid.
Did you know?
Put honey in the fridge, and it flows even more slowly!
Riddle time!
What has to be broken before you can use it?
An egg! Its shell is a solid, and inside is a runny liquid.
Your turn.
You can pour sand. Is sand a solid or a liquid?
Let's have a pouring race!
Put water, honey and shampoo on three spoons.
Tip the spoons at the same time.
Which liquid flows fastest? Which flows slowest?
Let's remember.
Solids keep their shape.
Liquids flow, and can be poured.
Liquids take the shape of their container.
And rice and sand are solids, made of tiny grains. Super scientists!

captions: Hello, material masters!
Solids and liquids can change.
This is lesson 3.3: melting and solidifying.
Have you ever had an ice cream on a hot day?
The sun heats the ice cream.
Drip, drip! It melts.
When a solid gets warm and turns into a liquid, it melts.
Now let's go the other way.
Pour some juice into a mould.
Put it in the freezer.
The cold juice turns into a solid lolly! A liquid turning into a solid is called solidifying, or freezing.
Pause and think.
What happens to chocolate when you hold it in a hot hand?
Lots of solids melt when they get hot.
Butter melts in a hot pan.
Chocolate melts in your warm hand.
Candle wax melts near the flame. Always ask an adult about candles.
Did you know?
Even rocks can melt, if they get hot enough.
Deep inside the Earth, rocks melt into lava!
Riddle time!
Ice cubes melt in a drink. What do they become?
Water!
Your turn.
What do we call it when a liquid turns into a solid?
Let's have an ice cube race!
Put one ice cube in a sunny place, and one in the shade.
Watch them carefully.
Which one melts first? Why?
Let's remember.
Heat makes solids melt into liquids.
Cooling makes liquids solidify into solids.
Solidifying is also called freezing.
And chocolate, butter and ice all melt when they get warm. Cool work!

q.prompt: Which is a sign that a chemical reaction has happened?

captions: Hello, kitchen chemists!
Sometimes materials change into something new.
This is lesson 3.4: chemical reactions.
Let's bake a cake.
We mix eggs, flour and sugar.
We heat it in the oven.
Now it is a cake! We cannot get the eggs back. A new material was made. This is a chemical reaction.
Pause and think.
Can you turn a cake back into eggs and flour?
Put some baking soda in a cup.
Add a little vinegar.
Fizz! Lots of bubbles!
The bubbles are a new gas. A chemical reaction happened.
How can you tell a reaction happened?
You might see bubbles.
The colour might change.
There might be heat or light, or a new smell.
Did you know?
When you peel a banana and leave it, it turns brown.
That is a chemical reaction with the air!
Riddle time!
What gets wetter, the more it dries?
A towel!
Your turn.
Which is a sign that a chemical reaction has happened?
Let's make a fizzy balloon. Ask an adult to help.
Put some vinegar in a bottle, and some baking soda in a balloon.
Fit the balloon over the bottle, and tip the baking soda in.
Watch! The gas blows up the balloon!
Let's remember.
A chemical reaction makes a new material.
Baking a cake is a chemical reaction.
Bubbles, colour changes, heat and new smells are signs of a reaction.
And most reactions cannot be undone. Excellent chemistry!
